name: Our Lady of Guadalupe
briefBio: Our Lady of Guadalupe is the December 12 Marian observance linked to the image and shrine at Tepeyac and the received tradition of Mary's encounters with Juan Diego in 1531. It is a universal optional memorial and, by a 1999 decree, a feast throughout the Americas, where Mary is invoked as patroness. The apparition narrative was first printed in Nahuatl in Luis Laso de la Vega's 1649 Huei tlamahuiçoltica; its Nican Mopohua section's authorship and composition date remain disputed. Earlier sixteenth-century records attest a shrine and image without narrating the encounters. Nahua rhetoric, collaborators, and later retellings reveal Indigenous interpretation, while contextual readings of Nahua documents prevent church or national stories from erasing local communities. The cloth venerated at the basilica belongs to received material tradition; art history studies it as a painted, altered colonial object rather than laboratory proof of supernatural origin. Guadalupe has served Indigenous, criollo, Mexican, and pan-American communities and has also been politically claimed. Devotion cannot guarantee cures, pregnancy, protection, or assent, essentialize race, stereotype Spaniards or Indigenous peoples, erase Indigenous communities, or become nationalist property.

sources.title: Decree concerning celebration of the Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Guadalupe throughout the American continent
sources.authorOrInstitution: Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments
sources.publisher: The Holy See, decree dated 25 March 1999
sources.reuseBasis: Formal decree used for the December 12 feast in every nation and territory of the Americas and patroness-of-all-America reception; continental rank is distinct from universal rank, and evangelization language is not used to glorify conquest or coercion

sources.title: Huei tlamahuiçoltica: Great Miracle of the Apparition of the Queen of Heaven, Saint Mary Our Beloved Mother of Guadalupe
sources.publisher: Mexico, 1649; digitized by the Library of Congress
sources.reuseBasis: Readable digitized primary Nahuatl printing used for the received apparition narrative, Juan Diego, Tepeyac, the bishop, ill uncle, roses, and image tradition; publication in 1649 does not by itself prove a 1531 event, earlier composition, Valeriano authorship, or miraculous material properties

sources.title: So That It May Come to the Attention of All the Indians: An Eighteenth-Century Sermon on the Virgin of Guadalupe and Juan Diego
sources.authorOrInstitution: Arthur J. O. Anderson and Barry D. Sell
sources.publisher: Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl 25 (1995), pp. 321–363, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México
sources.reuseBasis: Readable peer-reviewed Nahuatl study, especially the abstract and introductory textual history, used for the first securely dated Nahuatl apparition account in the 1649 Huei tlamahuiçoltica, the Nican Mopohua opening, and later Nahuatl preaching; it does not settle an earlier manuscript date or Valeriano authorship

sources.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe: The Origins and Sources of a Mexican National Symbol, 1531–1797, revised edition
sources.reuseBasis: Readable scholarly chapters used for Tepeyac traditions (chapter 2, pp. 27–34), witnesses through 1570 (chapter 4, pp. 50–73), the 1648–1649 published narratives (chapter 7, pp. 106–133), and colonial-to-national reception; its critical interpretation is not treated as the only scholarly verdict

sources.title: Guadalupan Nahua Stories: An Analysis of the Inner Indigenous Influence in Nahuatl Accounts of Guadalupe
sources.reuseBasis: Readable peer-reviewed study used at section 2 for dating and authorship debate and sections 3–9 for particular Nahuatl accounts, rhetorical forms, philology, multiple retellings, and Indigenous interpretation; no single essentialized Nahua worldview or biological racial claim is inferred

sources.title: Creating the Virgin of Guadalupe: The Cloth, the Artist, and Sources in Sixteenth-Century New Spain
sources.publisher: The Americas 61(4), 2005, pp. 571–610; Cambridge University Press; DOI 10.1017/S0003161500069327
sources.reuseBasis: Readable peer-reviewed article used especially at pp. 571–583 for the extant painted cloth, post-Conquest artistic production, mixed media, visual sources, material vulnerability, and later intervention; one reconstruction is not treated as final scientific consensus, and no miraculous material claim is made

sources.title: The Tira of Don Martín: A Living Nahua Chronicle
sources.authorOrInstitution: Alanna S. Radlo-Dzur, Mackenzie Cooley, Emily Kaplan, Leah Bright, E. Keats Webb, Mary Elizabeth Haude, Tana Villafana, and Amanda K. Satorius
sources.publisher: Latin American and Latinx Visual Culture 3(3), 2021, pp. 7–37; University of California Press; DOI 10.1525/lavc.2021.3.3.7
sources.reuseBasis: Full readable collaborative art-history and conservation study used at pp. 7–12 for document identity and locality and in the collected-and-studied-object analysis for multiple Nahua hands and layers, local property history, proof-mining of its Marian figure, and the authors' conclusion that no Guadalupe apparition connection is manifest

sources.title: Documentos Históricos
sources.authorOrInstitution: Instituto de Estudios Teológicos e Históricos Guadalupanos / Basilica of Santa María de Guadalupe
sources.publisher: Basílica de Santa María de Guadalupe
sources.reuseBasis: Official shrine reception used narrowly for living custody of Guadalupan archival traditions and the 1649 printed Huei tlamahuiçoltica; its settled Valeriano and circa-1556 claims conflict with independent chronology controls and are not used as proof of manuscript date, apparition, image science, or miraculous imprint

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 66–67: Christ Jesus — Mediator and Fullness of All Revelation
sources.reuseBasis: Formal doctrinal source used to distinguish private revelations from the deposit of faith and Christ's definitive public Revelation; it prevents treating an apparition tradition as an addition to or completion of public Revelation

sources.title: Liturgical Calendar: Universal Calendar — December
sources.authorOrInstitution: Liturgy Office, Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales
sources.publisher: Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales
sources.reuseBasis: Formal calendar used for Our Lady of Guadalupe on December 12 and universal optional-memorial rank; the page states that a celebration with no printed rank is an optional memorial, while the Americas feast comes from a separate decree and color comes from the GIRM

sources.title: General Instruction of the Roman Missal, nos. 345–346
sources.authorOrInstitution: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
sources.publisher: USCCB, Chapter VI: The Requisites for the Celebration of Mass
sources.reuseBasis: Formal liturgical norm used only for white at celebrations of the Blessed Virgin Mary; universal and continental rank come from separate calendar and decree evidence

editorial.reviewer: Catholic Daily factual and theological review

whyItMatters: Guadalupe joins Marian devotion, Nahuatl literary creativity, colonial material history, and contested public memory. Honest observance can protect Indigenous community agency and pan-American solidarity while refusing image science, racial stereotypes, cure guarantees, political ownership, and forced belief.
oneMinuteSummary: Our Lady of Guadalupe is the December 12 Marian observance associated with Tepeyac, its shrine, and a venerated painted cloth. The universal calendar lists an optional memorial; a 1999 decree makes the day a feast throughout the Americas and invokes Mary as the continent's patroness. The received 1531 apparition story was first printed in Nahuatl within the 1649 Huei tlamahuiçoltica. Its Nican Mopohua section's authorship and composition date remain disputed, while earlier records attest a shrine and image without that narrative. Nahua rhetoric, documents, collaborators, and local communities show interpretation and agency within colonial pressures. Material scholarship studies the image as painted cloth with artistic sources and interventions, not laboratory proof of supernatural origin. Guadalupe's colonial, Mexican, and pan-American reception is real but not exclusive property. Reject cure, pregnancy, protection, or conversion guarantees, coerced belief, racial stereotypes, political ownership, and erasure of Indigenous communities.

sections.heading: An observance with distinct calendar scopes
sections.body: Guadalupe is modeled as a Marian observance, not as a second biography of Juan Diego. December 12 is a universal optional memorial and a feast throughout the Americas, with white supplied by a separate liturgical norm.

sections.heading: The Nican Mopohua and early evidence
sections.body: The apparition story appears in the 1649 Nahuatl Huei tlamahuiçoltica. Nican Mopohua names its opening section; authorship and earlier dating remain contested. Sixteenth-century shrine and image testimony must not be silently turned into documentation of the full encounters.

sections.heading: Nahua documents and community agency
sections.body: Multiple Nahuatl retellings and layered Nahua documents reveal writers, artists, interpreters, property histories, and local communities. Context prevents selected imagery from swallowing Indigenous records into church or nationalist proof narratives.

sections.heading: Cloth, basilica, and later reception
sections.body: The basilica receives and preserves Guadalupan document and image traditions. Art history treats the venerated cloth as a vulnerable painted colonial object with mixed media and interventions. Criollo, Mexican, and pan-American uses belong to reception, not ownership or scientific proof.

life.gospelTheme: Mary's song directs devotion toward God's mercy, the dignity of the lowly, and justice without domination.
life.struggle: Guadalupe can be converted into laboratory proof, racial essence, colonial triumph, political property, or promises about health, pregnancy, and protection.
life.response: Receive the observance through Christ, label evidence honestly, center Indigenous community agency, and practice solidarity without coercion or guarantees.

virtues.name: Inculturated listening
virtues.evidence: Nahuatl accounts use Indigenous rhetorical and theological resources, while layered documents show communities interpreting and preserving their own local histories.
virtues.imitation: Invite a community to name its own symbols, needs, and language; compensate its interpreters and do not claim its voice as your evidence.

virtues.name: Hope without possession
virtues.evidence: Guadalupe became a major colonial, Mexican, and pan-American devotion, even as institutions and political movements competed over its meaning.
virtues.imitation: Support one Indigenous-led project without demanding religious, cultural, or political conformity.

practice.spiritual: Pray the Magnificat for communities whose language, land, labor, or history has been appropriated.
practice.action: Choose one Indigenous-led account of Guadalupe or local history, cite its creator, and correct one stereotype or unsupported miracle claim you encounter.

reflectionQuestions: Whose work and voice disappear when I tell the Guadalupe story?
Can I receive devotional hope without turning an image into scientific proof or Mary into political property?

scripture.connection: Mary's Magnificat keeps Guadalupe devotion oriented toward God's mercy, the lifting of the lowly, and justice rather than racial, colonial, or national supremacy.

prayer: God of mercy, in the observance of Our Lady of Guadalupe lead us to Christ and to one another. Honor Indigenous languages, artists, interpreters, families, and communities whose labor carries memory. Free us from stereotypes, coercion, political possession, false science, and promises of cures or protection. Make our devotion truthful, humble, and active in justice. Amen.
